recognition.where_to_look_first: The project set spans large fountain-form bunchgrasses, small tight bunchgrasses, creeping nimblewill, and rhizomatous low muhly. Start with growth form and scale, then inspect the ligule, leaf folding/rolling, and panicle size and openness.
priority: upright bunchgrass versus creeping/rooting or rhizomatous habit
flat versus folded or involute blades
open feathery versus narrow contracted panicle
spikelet size and awn detail when the habit split is not enough

quick_split: M. lindheimeri — large upright fountain-form bunchgrass with unusually long membranous ligules and a tall feathery panicle.
M. reverchonii — smaller compact bunchgrass with threadlike involute leaves and a delicate open reddish panicle.
M. schreberi — low weak creeping grass that roots at lower nodes; narrow contracted panicle.
M. utilis — short rhizomatous grass with creeping scaly rhizomes, filiform involute leaves, and a small narrow panicle.
M. ×involuta — dense upright bunchgrass with firm folded leaves and morphology intermediate between Lindheimer and seep muhly.
M. piniflora — keep visibly provisional; do not use as a final visual key until the source-name problem is resolved.
M. paniculata — installed pending taxonomy/photo review, not a genus-key teaching anchor until verified.
comparison_lesson.nursery_warning: Do not use pink plume color by itself to call a plant M. lindheimeri. The widely sold M. capillaris concept is not a project-native Central Texas anchor.

look_here_first: Start with HABIT: enormous fountain-form bunch or small fine rigid tuft or weak creeping stems? Compare dense narrow panicle versus airy branching. Next inspect fresh leaf/ligule with a hand lens and a mm scale. Neither pinkness nor nursery name proves species.

visual_comparison.title: Muhlenbergia — Lindheimer's dense fountain versus seep muhly's fine tuft
visual_comparison.subtitle: Four real photographs from existing learner galleries, inspected October 20. Arrows locate photographed panicles and clumps, not missing ligules or microscopic spikelets. The other five canonical Muhlenbergia concepts remain for subsequent visual work.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: LINDHEIMER = LARGE fountain + densely flowered tall panicle. SEEP = compact fine tuft + open delicate panicle. Both need ligule/spikelet photographs to confirm.

comparison_matrix.title: Two upright muhly bunchgrasses — strongest structures
rows: Habit
Large upright stiff fountain; often ca. 0.8–1.5 m
Compact, finer, often ca. 0.4–0.8 m
Full rooted plant with ruler; sizes overlap
Leaf blades
Longer relatively coarse, 2–5 mm in many treatments
Very fine threadlike, around 1–2 mm
Fresh blade and ruler; maturity matters
Flowering head
More contracted/densely flowered tall panicle
Open wispy branching panicle, sometimes reddish
Photograph panicle side by side and isolate spikelets
Ligule
Relatively long conspicuous membrane, GrassBase often 8–15 mm
Much shorter membrane in most treatments; some local length range disagreement
Measure in mm, do not infer from current photos
Tiny reproductive details
Usually one fertile floret; often short or absent lemma awn
Typically one fertile floret, awn often more evident
Dissect intact mature spikelets with scale
Pink coloration
May vary, not reliable
Can flush reddish, not reliable
Never ID from color alone
comparison_matrix.caution: UT Austin local seep muhly ligule length and broad GrassBase ranges differ; do not force absolute mm cutoffs. Growth size alone is supporting. M. capillaris is a nursery look-alike, not a project-local native anchor.
